poolDetails.name: twagner55's Bracket Pool
poolDetails.blurb: Try to correctly fill out this bracket for a chance to win a share of the prize pool!
poolDetails.gameTypeDescription: Fill out a tournament bracket, picking the winner of each game to advance

matchOutcomePickItemOutcomes.teamBlurb: This marks the Saints’ first tournament appearance since Fran McCaffery took the program to three straight dances from 2008 to 2010. The turnaround was pretty quick, too, considering coach Gerry McNamara added 10 wins in year one and nine more in year two. Sophomore guard Gavin Doty (17.9 PPG, 7.0 RPG) took a massive leap, while seniors Justice Shoats (13.2 PPG, 4.4 APG) and Brendan Coyle (8.6 PPG, 4.6 RPG) have continued to contribute as well. And with forward Antonio Chandler (7.3 PPG, 5.6 RPG) ruled ineligible by the NCAA at the very end of the regular season, Iowa transfer center Riley Mulvey stepped up with 11 points, 11 rebounds and five blocks in the MAAC title game. Siena committed the sixth-fewest fouls per game in the country this season and ranks in the top-third of tournament teams in two-point defense, plus their 65.7 points allowed per game ranked No. 15 nationally. However, their offense unfortunately owns the worst three-point percentage in the field.

Jon Scheyer has not allowed the Duke standard to slip to any extent since taking over as head coach, and this is shaping up to be his best team yet. The Blue Devils enter the NCAA Tournament with a 32-2 overall record, ranked No. 1 in the AP poll, and are the winners of the ACC Conference Tournament to earn the outright top seed. Cameron Boozer (22.5 PPG, 10.2 RPG, 4.2 APG) has a strong case for the best player in the country, and Duke gets the job done on both sides of the ball. The Blue Devils rank 48th in the country in scoring, third in opponents’ points allowed, and in the top seven in both offensive and defensive ratings. Injuries to Caleb Foster (8.5 PPG and 3.6 RPG) and Patrick Ngongba (10.7 PPG and 6.0 RPG) are a notable storyline to watch. However, the Blue Devils’ depth deserves credit for embodying the next-man-up mentality. When Duke plays to its peak, it looks like the best team in the country. The Blue Devils will look to put this on display throughout their NCAA Tournament run.

The season looked like it was going to be a disaster for the Horned Frogs out of the gates, losing their season opener as a 21.5-point favorite to New Orleans. But that game turned out to be an outlier for a TCU team that went on to collect wins over Florida, Wisconsin, Iowa State and Texas Tech, not to mention taking Michigan and Kansas (twice) right down to the wire. TCU was on the bubble about a month ago, but removed any doubt by ripping off nine wins over its last 10 games, until running into Kansas in the Big 12 Tournament. Jamie Dixon’s Horned Frogs could be a complete wild card in March, given that they’ve shorn the ability to compete with many of the best teams in the country, while also being capable of taking a loss to some of the worst teams in the nation. It’s the defense that allows TCU to hang around in any given matchup, ranking 22nd in defensive efficiency on KenPom.

The Buckeyes were considered a bubble team just a couple weeks ahead of Selection Sunday, but won their first four games in March, including an upset over Purdue. Ohio State fell short in the Big Ten Tournament, but lost a competitive game to Michigan. Entering the NCAA Tournament, the Buckeyes rank 17th in offensive efficiency on KenPom. Given their recent success against teams like Michigan and Purdue at the top of the Big Ten, the Buckeyes have the offensive firepower to compete with anybody in the country. But Ohio State has to get hot if it's going to make a run in March. When Ohio State isn’t clicking on offense, the defense and rebounding haven’t been good enough to win games on their own. Senior guard Bruce Thornton has been the engine that makes that offense go, averaging over 20 points on the season while shooting 40% from downtown.

The Panthers may be making their first appearance in the NCAA tournament in a decade, but coach Ben Jacobson is still heading up the program. He led Northern Iowa to tournament wins in 2015 and 2016, not to mention his Sweet 16 appearance with the team back in 2010. As a result, Jacobson is running a bit of an old-school program out in Cedar Falls, with only one of his 12 players suiting up for another college last season. Senior guard Trey Campbell (13.7 PPG) epitomizes the team’s continuity, donning purple and gold in all 133 of his collegiate appearances. While Leon Bond III (11.9 PPG), Will Hornseth (11.2 PPG) and Ben Schwieger (9.2 PPG) can each pour it in as well, the Panthers’ strongest asset is their defense. Northern Iowa allowed the fewest points per game in the country this season (61.3 PPG), as well as the third-lowest three-point percentage (28.5%). No team in the field runs at a slower adjusted pace than the Panthers, either, so they can really drag teams into the mud. A 6-9 stretch during MVC sunk what could have been an otherwise solid resume, but they did heat back up in the conference tournament and win each of their last six road and neutral site contests.

Rick Pitino has led St. John’s to a 28-6 record this season, which includes winning the Big East with an 18-2 conference record and taking down Connecticut to win the Big East Tournament Championship. The Red Storm enter the NCAA Tournament having won 19 of their past 20 games, with the lone loss coming against UConn. They finished the year ranked 13th in the AP Poll, 58th in scoring, 72nd in opponents’ points allowed, and in the top 80 in both offensive and defensive rating. Zuby Ejiofor (16.3 PPG and 7.1 RPG) and Bryce Hopkins (13.5 PPG and 6.2 RPG) headline the production. This is a team that has gotten better as the season has progressed and has a head coach with as much NCAA Tournament experience as you could ask for. You can critique their 223rd-ranked three-point percentage or some inconsistent point guard play, but the Red Storm will bring their best effort in every matchup they draw and be a tough out in this tournament.

Cal Baptist should scare the bracket favorites a little. The Lancers are 25-8, won the WAC tournament, and earned the program’s first NCAA tournament berth in the Division I era after a delirious closing weekend in Las Vegas. Their first matchup is Kansas in the East Region’s 4-13 game, which is exactly the sort of stage where a team like this gets to find out whether months of discipline can pass for menace under brighter lights. The Lancers average 73.0 points, 39.9 rebounds, and 5.5 blocks per game, and the more revealing advantage is on defense: opponents shot just 41.7% from the field, 29.7% from three, and posted only a 46.4% effective field goal rate against them. Cal Baptist also ranked 50th nationally in adjusted defensive efficiency at KenPom, which is another way of saying this team knows how to make a favorite work for every clean look. Dominique Daniels Jr. is the headline actor here at 23.2 points and 3.2 assists per game, and he spent championship weekend playing like a man trying to kick the door off its hinges—41 against Utah Tech in the semifinal, then 23 in the 63-61 title-game win over Utah Valley, including the Lancers’ final nine points. Martel Williams adds 12.7 a night, Jordan Muller gives them secondary shooting, and the tournament hope is obvious: turn this into a defensive argument, let Daniels own the late possessions, and make Kansas feel the game tightening instead of floating. Cal Baptist does not need a long run to matter. One real scare, one ugly upset bid, maybe one full theft—that is enough to turn a first appearance into a proper March introduction.

The Kansas program maintains a reputation as one of the sport’s blue bloods, but following a National Championship in March of 2022, the Jayhawks haven’t advanced past the second round in any of the last three seasons. Perhaps Darryn Peterson can help change that after averaging 19.8 points per game as one of the more intriguing pro prospects in this tournament, but the Jayhawks have a very solid team around him for the most part. They’re 21st in the KenPom rankings with the 10th-best DRTG in the nation, holding opponents to the fourth-lowest eFG%. Beyond that, they’re strong on the glass at 24th in rebounding, but questions about the offense’s capabilities are worth asking—Kansas averages just 75.6 PPG and ranks 57th in ORTG.

The Bulls are another program that favors a boat-race approach to the game. The funny part is that it worked, getting them to the top of the American Conference with a 25-8 overall record and 15-3 conference mark before ultimately hoisting hardware to earn the autobid. USF averages 87.0 PPG, sixth in the nation, overwhelming opponents through the sheer volume of the third-most FGA per contest. The efficiency is nothing to write home about, but there have been some wild outputs on the scoreboard with 15 outings of 90-plus points with six 100-point performances among that sample. Wes Enis brings 16.7 PPG with Izaiyah Nelson posting 15.8 points with 9.7 boards, plus three other players are in the double digits. The Bulls are also fourth in rebounds per game with 42.5, another major boon for this roster. The most intriguing aspect? While one could say USF eschews defense by allowing 76.3 PPG, the team actually ranks 47th in the nation in opponent eFG% and is 11th in steals per game. That inflated scoring total conceded to opponents is more a product of pace than lack of prowess, which is reflected at 47th in the KenPom rankings and 40th in DRTG.

Louisville’s hard to figure out, and even harder when you consider its rocky February. The Cardinals are 23-10, went 11-7 in the ACC, and are a No. 6 seed with the program still hunting its first NCAA tournament win in nearly a decade. The numbers say this is a ceiling squad: 84.7 points per game, 47% shooting, 35.7% from three, 76.9% at the line, 38.5 rebounds, 17.1 assists, and 6.9 steals. Their official totals also imply about a 56.4% effective field goal rate, which is serious offense by any standard, and they pair it with opponents held to 42.4% shooting overall and 32.7% from deep. The roster has the shape of a team that can look top-20 for 20 minutes, and then spend the next 20 reminding everybody why March is not obliged to honor potential. Ryan Conwell is at 18.7 points with 105 made threes; Mikel Brown Jr. has 18.2 points and 4.7 assists in 21 games; J’Vonne Hadley gives them 11.8 points, 5.2 rebounds, and 45.6% from three; Sananda Fru has been a devastatingly efficient interior piece at 9.2 points, 6.0 rebounds, 1.4 blocks, and 75.9% from the field. The recent form is the whole tension of the blurb: Louisville survived SMU 62-58 in the ACC tournament without Brown, then lost 78-73 to Miami in a game where the Cardinals coughed it up 13 times and shot just 6-for-24 from three. That is the anxiety and the promise in one frame. If Brown is healthy enough to keep the creation honest and limit the turnovers, Louisville has too much perimeter shotmaking to be a casual out.

North Dakota State is one of those mid-major entries that looks modest until you actually start reading the stat sheet. Then you realize the operation is impressively complete. The Bison are at 27-7 and first in the Summit, and the broader profile is balanced in the way tournament underdogs need to be: 80.7 points per game, 69.6 allowed, 15.5 assists, and enough shooting to keep a favorite from loading up on one option. North Dakota State shot 46.8% from the field and 36.5% from three, averaged 9.4 made threes per game, posted a 53.4% effective field goal rate and 1.126 shooting efficiency, rebounded 32.0% of its own misses, cleared 76.4% of defensive boards, and kept its turnover rate to 13.3% of possessions Damari Wheeler-Thomas leads them with 14.4 points per game, Trevian Carson adds 12.0 points and 6.4 rebounds, Andy Stefonowicz averages 4.9 assists, and the roster has real scoring spread beyond the marquee names. Their first matchup is Michigan State, which is both a brutal draw and a strangely appropriate one—Tom Izzo on the other sideline, a disciplined three seed, a game that will demand adult possessions from the opening tip. But the reason North Dakota State is interesting is that it does own a few receipts that hint at live-underdog potential, including a 99-94 nonconference win at Drake and the Summit title-clincher over North Dakota. The tournament hopes here are necessarily modest. This team needs its spacing, ball movement, and guard shotmaking to make Michigan State uncomfortable for long enough that the bracket pressure starts to feel reciprocal. That is a very possible script. It is just one that requires nearly perfect timing.

An 88-84 defeat to UCLA ended Michigan State’s time in the Big Ten Tournament. Still, legendary head coach Tom Izzo usually has his guys ready for the gauntlet that is March Madness. This is your classic Sparty roster, built on defense and basketball IQ. The main catalyst on offense is Jeremy Fears Jr., who leads the Big Ten with 9.2 assists per game. Big man Jaxon Kohler is another name to watch as well (12.7 PPG, 9.0 RPG). A slow-paced, grind-it-out approach works out over the course of the regular season. However, it can deliver mixed results at this time of year. MSU doesn’t take many three-pointers, ranking 240th in 3PA/FGA on KenPom. That’s not a bad thing per se, but it does mean the Spartans need to remain efficient from inside the arc. Still, should anyone count out Izzo, aka Mr. March? Probably not.

The Knights started the season 12-1, jumping into the AP Top 25 for the first time in seven years after a win over Kansas. UCF proceeded to alternate between three-game winning streaks and three-game losing streaks, though, ending the year 7-6 in neutral and away contests. UCF leans heavily on its veteran backcourt duo of Riley Kugel (14.4 PPG, 39.2% 3PT) and Themus Fulks (14.1 PPG, 6.7 APG). The Knights have plenty of length in the frontcourt, namely in the form of 7-foot-2 sophomore John Bol. In just 18.7 minutes a night, Bol averages 6.0 points, 5.5 rebounds and 1.1 blocks per game. Forwards Jordan Burks and Jamichael Stillwell average 24.7 points and 12.8 rebounds per game between them, too. UCF ranks No. 17 among tournament teams in three-point percentage.

Mick Cronin’s Bruins had an elite season at home, notching wins over three top-10 teams: Purdue, Illinois and Nebraska. Their travels were far less successful. In the regular season, UCLA went 1-6 playing outside of the Pacific time zone, which isn't very promising considering it wound up in the East Region. The Bruins turned that around a bit in the Big Ten Tournament in Chicago, fending off Rutgers and upsetting Michigan State. They even took the Boilermakers down to the wire without leading stars Tyler Bilodeau (17.6 PPG, 65.6% TS) and Donovan Dent (13.5 PPG, 7.6 APG). Both players are expected to be healthy in time for the Round of 64, sparking an offense that ranks No. 2 in adjusted efficiency since Feb. 18. Dent, especially, was on a tear with 77 assists, 10 steals and 6 turnovers in the seven games leading up to his calf injury. The Bruins went 13-0 in Quad 3 and 4 games, but just 10-11 against Quad 1 and 2 opponents thanks to an uncharacteristically mediocre Cronin defense that ranks No. 54 in KenPom.

After a middling run through conference play that featured an 0-3 record in overtime contests, the Paladins ran the table in the Southern tournament and knocked off regular season champ East Tennessee State. The program’s only holdover from their 2023 tournament team is forward Ben VanderWal, who got demoted out of the starting five last week. Instead, coach Bob Richey has been leaning more on fresh blood, namely freshman guard Alex Wilkins (17.7 PPG, 4.7 APG) and Clemson transfer forward Asa Thomas (12.4 PPG, 38.9% 3PT). Junior big man Cooper Bowser (14.0 PPG, 6.0 RPG, 1.1 BPG) has also held his own since missing over a month of action due to injury. Furman ranks No. 10 among tournament teams in three-point rate, but 10th-to-last in three-point percentage. The Paladins are far more successful inside the arc, where they rank No. 8 in shooting percentage. And while their free throw rate differential is good for No. 14 in the field, their turnover differential is the fifth-worst.

After back-to-back national championships in 2022-23 and 2023-24, the Connecticut Huskies have re-tooled and are intent on making some noise this season. Dan Hurley’s squad finished with a 29-5 record but fell to St. John’s in the Big East Tournament Championship. Alex Karaban (12.6 PPG and 5.2 RPG) continues to play a valuable role as he did on both championship teams, while Tarris Reed Jr. (13.7 PPG and 8.1 RPG), Solo Ball (13.5 PPG), Braylon Mullins (12 PPG), and Silas Demary Jr. (10.9 PPG and 6.2 RPG) each also play key roles. Connecticut held opponents to the 11th fewest points per game this season and ranks in the top 23 in opponents’ field goal and three-point percentage. The Huskies are battle-tested, know their identity as a basketball team, and aren’t afraid of any opponent. Hurley demands perfection and will let everyone in the arena hear about it if this is not the case.

The defending national champions looked like the team to beat once again heading into Saturday. That was prior to Vanderbilt’s shocking 91-74 victory in the SEC Tournament semifinals. Still, it would be foolish to count out this battle-tested Florida squad. Head coach Todd Golden has built a monster, especially inside the paint. Florida leads all of college basketball with a 59.5% total rebounding percentage. The Gators have not one, not two, but three weapons on the glass: Thomas Haugh (6.2 RPG), Alex Condon (7.7 RPG) and SEC Defensive Player of the Year Rueben Chinyelu (11.5 RPG). In the back court, Boogie Fland and Xaivian Lee are difference-makers as well. Prior to the Vanderbilt loss, Florida had reeled off 12 straight wins. All signs are pointing to another deep tournament run for this group.

It didn’t take first-year coach Ben McCollum to get the Hawkeyes back on track, picking up right where he left off at Drake. Even a three-game losing streak in early January didn’t stop Iowa from getting off to an 18-5 start. At the same time, they enter the Big Dance on a 3-7 skid, having lost 5 of their last 6 games away from home. McCollum’s extremely balanced squad boasts the second-slowest pace in the field, on top of ranking No. 31 in adjusted offensive rating and No. 30 in adjusted defensive rating. Bennett Stirtz was plenty familiar with McCollum’s system, following him from Des Moines to Iowa City and immediately averaging 20.0 points per game. Forward Cooper Koch is the only other high-volume perimeter shooter in the rotation, which boasts eight players averaging at least 5.0 points per game. The fundamentally-sound Hawkeyes’ defining stats are turnover differential and effective field goal percentage, where they rank No. 6 and No. 9 among tournament teams, respectively. Now Iowa just has to prove that those figures can travel when the stakes are the highest.

Brad Brownell has assembled a stellar defensive unit, which has been the blueprint to Clemson’s success this season. The Tigers finished the year with a 24-10 record, which includes some tough wins over teams like North Carolina, Louisville, SMU, and Georgia. Clemson ranks 229th in scoring, but 28th in opponents' points allowed. They also rank 53rd in defensive rating, 57th in opponents’ field goal percentage, and 17th in offensive rebounds allowed. RJ Godfrey (11.9 points and 5.3 rebounds) and Carter Welling (10.2 points and 5.4 rebounds) are the only players averaging in double figures. They lean more on their depth, with seven players averaging 6.2 points per game or greater and eight if you count Zac Foster, who suffered a season-ending ACL tear. However, no player on the roster shoots above 35.4% on three-point attempts (minimum 30 3PA). If Clemson can control the tempo and play a defensive-oriented battle, they are capable of beating anyone. But there are some notable offensive limitations, and they do not rebound as well as you would hope for a team of this profile.

The pride and joy of Southland Conference basketball, McNeese State catapulted into the national mainstream with back-to-back March Madness appearances in the last two years. While Will Wade left for NCST, Bill Armstrong took over to coach this team to a 28-5 finish and 19-3 mark in conference play, also winning the Southland tourney. The Cowboys admittedly played an easy schedule given their conference, but a spot at 68th per KenPom still means something. The defense is where they’re better with 67.0 PPG allowed and the 49th-ranked DRTG, while their 10.3 steals per game are second-most in the nation. Plus, it’s tough to rule out this offense, too. McNeese averages 76.8 PPG primarily behind the efforts of Larry Johnson (17.5 PPG) and Tyshawn Archie (14.3 PPG). However, there’s still something to be said about being less battle-tested than the bigger fish in the field.

Vanderbilt has the look of a team that spent all winter building an indefensible castle, only to reach Selection Sunday and find out the committee still preferred the old hierarchies. The Commodores are 26-8, got shoved onto the No. 5 line in the South, and draw McNeese in Oklahoma City despite a profile that screamed something cleaner: a NET sitting at 13, a KenPom standing better than multiple No. 4 seeds, and a 10-6 mark in Quad 1 games. The numbers on the floor are just as loud. Vanderbilt enters the tournament with a school-record-tying 26 wins, an offense that has lived in the 90s for stretches, and a lead guard-wing combination that feels made for tense first-weekend possessions. Tyler Tanner is the leading scorer at 19.2 points per game with 5.3 assists and 2.4 steals, Duke Miles adds 16.4 points and 4.3 assists while shooting nearly 90% from the line, and Tyler Nickel spaces the whole thing with 13.3 points and 39.1% shooting from three. The recent receipts are strong too: two wins over Tennessee in eight days and a 91-74 demolition of Florida in the SEC tournament semifinal. So the tournament hope is obvious. McNeese is dangerous enough to make the opener sweaty, but Vanderbilt’s ceiling is at least the second weekend if the shotmaking travels and the draw stays honest.

Troy’s tournament outlook is the sort of thing March is built to test: a solid, bruising, slightly anonymous champion asked to bother a program that still carries a giant piece of historical nervousness into the room. The Trojans are 22-11, went 12-6 in the Sun Belt, and got the auto bid out of a conference that spent all season behaving like a fight in a stairwell. Their numbers are respectable without being gaudy—80.3 points per game, 38.3 rebounds, 16 assists, 73.1 points allowed—and the advanced stats helps explain the personality a little better: Troy shot 44.6% from the field and 33.9% from three, averaged 16.1 made free throws per game at a 72.3% clip, posted a +3.5 rebounding margin, forced 8.0 steals per game, carried a 1.3 assist-turnover ratio, and scored 18.5 points off turnovers. Victor Valdes leads them with 14.8 points and 4.6 assists per game, while Thomas Dowd controls the interior with 10.1 rebounds a night. There is a weird little warning flare in Troy’s season log: the Trojans scored 106 in a wild triple-overtime loss at USC, which at least suggests they are not allergic to big-stage volatility. The ceiling is still probably one game.

The Nebraska Cornhuskers are 26-6 on the season and finished the year ranked 11th in the AP Poll. Fred Hoiberg’s squad has a high-level defense that ranks 22nd in opponents’ points allowed, 22nd in defensive rating, 22nd in opponents’ field goal percentage, and 11th in opponents’ three-point percentage. Offensively, they are a bit lacking in overall firepower but rank 14th in three-point attempts per game, 14th in assists per game, and take excellent care of the basketball. Pryce Sandfort (17.8 PPG and 4.8 RPG) headlines the production while shooting 40.1% on three-pointers. Rienk Mast (13.5 PPG and 5.8 RPG) and Braden Frager (11.6 PPG and 3.8 RPG) also average in double figures. After getting off to a 20-0 start to the season, Nebraska lost six of its final 12 games. But the Cornhuskers have a pair of ranked wins over Michigan State and Illinois, and have showcased a high level of play throughout the season.

Despite the popular opinion that the Rams would get an at-large big if they happened to lose in the Atlantic 10 Tournament, the Selection Committee revealed that they would have been left out of the NCAA Tournament field had they not defeated Dayton in the A-10 Championship game. VCU has been incredibly balanced all season, ranking 42nd in offensive efficiency and 60th in defensive efficiency on KenPom, while also ranking 88th nationally in rebound rate. The Rams have lost the majority of the games they’ve played against NCAA Tournament level competition, with their best non-conference win over South Florida. VCU also dropped games to Utah State, New Mexico, NC State and Vanderbilt. That said, arguably nobody in the country is hotter than VCU, which has posted a 16-1 record since January 14 entering NCAA Tournament play.

The Tar Heels were 20-5 overall and 8-4 in ACC play prior to Valentine’s Day, but leading scorer Caleb Wilson suffered a hand injury that would sideline him for the next few games before a broken thumb sustained in practice ended his season. In the absence of the forward and his 19.8 points per game, North Carolina went 5-3 and eventually fell short in the opening round of the conference tourney. Big man Henri Veesaar has performed admirably in a featured role with 16.7 points and 8.7 boards per game, and Seth Trimble pitches in 14 PPG as well. Still, UNC’s ceiling isn’t the same as it once was. The program now sits 29th in the KenPom rankings at 32nd in ORTG and 37th in DRTG, but averages only 73.4 PPG without Wilson, over six PPG fewer than its full-season sample.

After starting the season 9-10, the Quakers came alive when it mattered most. Penn is 9-1 over its last 10, beating a top-100 Yale team in the Ivy League title game on Sunday. The Quakers were able to do that without forward Ethan Roberts, who missed the conference tournament with a concussion. If Penn gets Roberts back, that’s 16.9 points per game and 40.4% three-point shooting to help pull off an upset. Forward TJ Power was an All-Ivy honoree with 15.8 points and 7.6 rebounds per game, shooting 42.7% from deep. Thanks to that duo, the Quakers rank No. 19 in the country in three-point percentage.

Do you like offense? Look no further than Illinois, one of the most exciting teams in this year’s bracket. Brad Underwood has put together another juggernaut, ranking second on KenPom in adjusted offensive efficiency (131.2). The squad fell short during the Big Ten Tournament, however, getting bounced by Wisconsin in overtime. In fact, the Illini have dropped five of their last nine contests. Getting back on track is no guarantee, but this school certainly has the pieces to make it happen. Five different players are averaging at least 10 points per game, led by freshman phenom Keaton Wagler (17.9 PPG). There’s experience here as well, with upperclassmen Kylan Boswell (13.2 PPG) and Andrej Stojakovic (13.4 PPG). Down low, David Mirkovic (13.4 PPG) and seven-footers Tomislav and Zvonimir Ivisic can wreak havoc. Maintaining effort on defense, along with consistent shooting, are the key factors for a potential Final Four appearance.

There are a handful of teams in this bracket that are of the “all gas, no brakes” ilk when it comes to game plans. Texas A&M is one of them, averaging the fourth-most PPG of any program at 87.7 but allowing a whopping 79.6 PPG on the other end of the floor. The Aggies come in at 39th in the KenPom rankings having gone 21-11 overall and 11-7 against SEC foes. They can clearly score with anyone and are surprisingly efficient despite ranking 29th in adjusted tempo and sixth in FGA per game – a 45.8% FG% is perfectly fine, a 36.2% 3P% falls 47th, and a 1.671 AST/TO ratio comes in at 17th. Rashaun Agee’s 14.7 PPG and 8.9 boards lead the team, which has four other double-digit scorers. Just get ready for a shootout environment in every game this group plays… Texas A&M may not win otherwise.

Randy Bennett’s squad earned an outright NCAA Tournament bid by going 27-5 in the regular season and climbing to 21st in the AP Poll. Saint Mary’s has one of the best defenses in the country, ranking seventh in opponents' points allowed, 18th in defensive rating, and 24th in opponents’ field goal percentage. The Gaels were eliminated by Santa Clara in the West Coast Conference tournament, which snapped an eight-game winning streak. They defeated Gonzaga in the previous matchup, but this marks their lone ranked victory of the season. Paulius Muraskas (18.8 points and 7.7 rebounds) headlines the production, while Mikey Lewis (14.2 points) and Joshua Dent (13.0 points and 5.7 assists) also play key roles. They have some offensive limitations, ranking 116th in the country in scoring at 78.2 points per game, but they shoot three-pointers at the 10th-best efficiency in the country and are one of the best rebounding teams in the country. Saint Mary’s has increasingly become an NCAA Tournament staple in recent years, and this season has shaped up to be one of their most impressive overall units.

The Vandals finished the regular season at 17-14, which was only good for seventh in the Big Sky. They barely snuck by Montana State in the conference quarterfinals, then rose to the occasion against both Eastern Washington and Montana to earn the automatic bid to March Madness—their first since 1990. Idaho has four players who can step up and catalyze the offense between Jackson Rasmussen (13.9 PPG), Kolton Mitchell (13.7 PPG), Biko Johnson (12.4 PPG), and Isaiah Brickner (12.1). Six-foot-11 senior Brody Rowbury leads the team with 5.2 boards per night. The Vandals rank in the top 100 nationally in three-point percentage, while limiting opponent offensive rebounds better than all but seven other programs.

Kelvin Sampson has established an identity in Houston by playing with plenty of grit, high-level defense, and fighting for every loose ball. This year’s team checks every single box for what you would hope for in a peak Houston team, with some offensive flashes above what is typically expected. The Cougars went 28-6 on the season and fell just short against Arizona in the Big 12 Tournament Championship. Star freshman guard Kingston Flemings (16.4 points and 5.3 assists) headlines the production, while Emanuel Sharp (15.3 PPG) is in his senior season, and Milos Uzan (11.1 PPG) also brings some experience. Houston is holding teams to the second-fewest points per game in the country, and there is little doubt that its defense is of national championship quality. It is to be determined if its offense will be enough, but this is a team that no opponent should desire facing in this type of high-intensity setting.

The Michigan Wolverines looked like the gold standard of college basketball for most of the season, and don’t let this seeming slip in hype confuse you with vulnerability. Michigan attacked the transfer portal aggressively and has an experienced squad that plays at a high level together. Yaxel Lendeborg (14.4 PPG and 7.0 RPG), Morez Johnson Jr. (13.3 PPG and 7.3 RPG), and Aday Mara (11.6 PPG, 6.9 RPG and 2.6 BPG) dominate the interior, while Elliot Cadeau (10.2 PPG and 5.4 APG) and Trey McKenney (9.7 PPG) can each carry the team for stretches in the backcourt. Dusty May’s group scores at the 10th-best rate in the country, ranks 56th in opponents’ points allowed, and is in the top 13 in both offensive and defensive ratings. The Wolverines are 31-2 on the season, finished third in the AP Poll, and fell just short to Purdue in the Big Ten Conference Championship. Michigan can win games in a variety of ways, and this is the moment it has waited for all year.

The Billikens got an at-large bid out of the Atlantic 10 for their full body of work, but have not been playing their best basketball over the last month. Saint Louis began the season with a record of 24-1, and the lone loss was by a single point to Stanford on a neutral floor. Over the last month, Saint Louis has gone just 4-4. The Billikens play with rapid tempo, and are an exciting team to watch, led by A-10 POY Robbie Avila. Saint Louis ranked 11th nationally in scoring this season, entering the NCAA Tournament putting up an average of 86.4 points per game. The Billikens also are among the nation’s elite in rebound rate. Even though they are limping into the tournament without any momentum, the Billikens are capable of being a tough matchup for anybody.

Georgia enters the tournament like a team that made the field by leaning into modern excess. The Bulldogs are 22-10, finished 10-8 in the SEC, and play an extremely watchable, slightly unstable kind of basketball: 89.8 points per game, 38.2 rebounds, just under 15 assists, and 79.2 points allowed. In other words, Georgia lives in games that feel a little too loud. Jeremiah Wilkinson is the headline scorer at 17.0 points per game, Marcus Millender runs the table with 4.0 assists, and Somtochukwu Cyril gives the front line formidable defensive shape with 2.3 blocks while shooting 76.4% from the field. Their first matchup is Saint Louis in the 8-9 game, which is exactly the sort of opener that can either validate a season or turn it into an asterisk. Georgia’s tournament hopes are built on offensive pressure—on the belief that its pace, guard scoring, and shot volume can make a disciplined opponent blink first. But the danger is obvious too: teams that defend like this do not always get to choose the temperature in March. The optimistic read is that Georgia has enough juice to win one and make this feel like a proper arrival season. The colder read is that a likely second-round meeting with top-seeded Michigan would expose every shaky possession on the other end. Georgia is live, but live in the way a spark is live—not in the way a bonfire is.

Akron has become one of those programs that no longer feels like a cute conference story and instead feels like an annual operational threat. The Zips are 29-5, went 17-1 in the MAC, won the league tournament for the third straight year, and once again arrive with an offense that looks built to make a higher seed profoundly uncomfortable: 88.4 points per game, 18.4 assists—17th nationally—and enough shot creation to keep possessions from dying ugly deaths. Akron ranks fifth nationally in offensive efficiency at 1.192 points per possession, sits eighth in effective field goal percentage at 58.5%, shoots 59.1% on twos and 38.5% from three, posts a 61.7% true shooting mark, and turns it over only 10.4 times per game while carrying a 125.7 offensive rating. Tavari Johnson is the engine at 20.1 points and 5.0 assists per game, while Amani Lyles adds 14.6 points and shoots 55.7% from the field. Their first matchup is the classic 12-5 pressure point, against Texas Tech, and that is exactly the sort of bracket real estate where Akron’s reputation starts humming. This is a team that plays fast without feeling wild, and experienced without feeling old. Its tournament hopes are immediate. The first weekend is the whole pitch. Upset the five, and suddenly the conversation around Akron changes from nice mid-major repeat customer to genuine bracket actor. The longer-range ceiling is still modest because the Midwest turns brutal in a hurry, but the Zips don’t need a Final Four fantasy to matter. They just need one of those March afternoons where the favorite keeps looking up and realizing the score is still wrong. Akron has been rehearsing that scene for years.

The Red Raiders advanced to the Elite Eight last year but ultimately fell short to the eventual national champs. They returned with a vengeance this season and looked like they might contend for the Big 12 title … until disaster struck as star JT Toppin suffered a season-ending torn ACL, leaving Texas Tech without its leading scorer and rebounder (21.8 PPG, 10.8 RPG). The Red Raiders finished the regular season 22-10 overall and 12-6 in conference play, but went just 3-3 in Toppin’s absence. Granted, the group remains feisty with an attack centered around perimeter play, shooting 39.3% from beyond the arc with the fourth-most 3PM per game. Star guard Christian Anderson has stepped up in a big way with 18.9 points and 7.6 assists a night, but it’s unclear whether he can carry the load as the primary option. Things just look shaky without Toppin, so even at 20th on KenPom’s rankings, the upside of this roster may be capped.

A quarter-century later, Hofstra is back in the NCAA Tournament. The Pride went 24–10 and 12–6 in the CAA, winning 11 of their last 12 games en route to a conference title — beating Monmouth, 75–69, in Tuesday’s finale. The squad clinched the 13th seed in the Midwest Region, looking for its first March Madness win in program history against No. 4 Alabama in Tampa on Friday. CAA Player of the Year Cruz Davis leads the conference with 20.2 points per game, and CAA Rookie of the Year Preston Edmead adds 15.9 points of his own. But the team’s true calling card is on the other end: Hofstra ranks 29th nationally in rebounds per game, 19th in points allowed, and fourth in opponent field-goal percentage. Their defense will be put to the ultimate test against the Crimson Tide, who lead the country in scoring.

If you are a fan of offense, then Alabama is the team for you. Nate Oats’ squad leads the country in scoring at 91.7 points per game and has scored at least 100 points in eight games this year. The Crimson Tide rank 10th in offensive rating and launch more three-point attempts than any team in the country. While their defense leaves plenty to be desired, Alabama’s impressive scoring has led them to a 23-9 record, which includes ranked wins over St. John’s, Illinois, Arkansas and Tennessee. Labaron Philon (21.7 PPG and 4.7 APG) leads the offensive charge, while Aden Holloway (16.8 PPG and 3.8 APG) and Latrell Wrightsell Jr. (12.8 PPG and 3.1 RPG) are also major factors. The phrase “defense wins championships” is clearly not one the Crimson Tide subscribes to, but they will challenge every opponent to put up points at a high rate. This high-paced offensive style inherently leads to some additional variance, but when Alabama is playing to its peak, it can beat anyone in the country.

Tennessee’s bracket is a Rick Barnes mood special—hard edges, anxious silence, a defense that keeps trying to turn every game into a locked room. The Volunteers are 22-11, landed on the No. 6 line in the Midwest, and will not even meet their first-round opponent until Miami (Ohio) and SMU finish their First Four fight in Dayton. That is a very Tennessee entry point into March: no clean reveal, no warm lighting, just another demand that the defense make the whole evening ugly enough to matter. And the underlying numbers still sell that identity. Tennessee scored 79.5 points per game and allowed 69.4, but the more revealing layer is the possession math: 46.3% from the field, 52.2% on twos, a 51.6% effective field goal rate, a 42.6-29.8 rebounding split, 16.9 assists against 11.7 turnovers, and opponents held to 40.9% shooting overall and 30.6% from three. Even the shot map tells the same story—the Vols force opponents into a ton of perimeter volume without giving away clean percentages, which is how a game starts to feel airless in a hurry. Ja’Kobi Gillespie is the system’s pulse at 18 points, 5.5 assists, 88 made threes, and a 2.4-to-1 assist-turnover ratio. Nate Ament is the elastic two-way answer at 17.5 points, 6.6 rebounds, 76 assists, 32 steals, 17 blocks, and 232 free-throw attempts in 31 games—a foul-drawing wing who can still make the floor feel bigger and meaner at the same time. Felix Okpara gives them the interior deterrence piece at 58.8% shooting, 6.2 rebounds, and 44 blocks, while Tennessee as a team still wobbles at the line just enough—69.4%—to keep the old March anxiety alive. The Auburn game remains the most persuasive recent receipt: a 20-0 run, more than seven straight minutes of defensive suffocation, and a version of Tennessee that looked like it could drag almost anyone into a bad dream. That is the hope and the warning. Everybody can picture the Vols in the Sweet 16. Nobody ever pictures the route as comfortable.

Wright State returns to the NCAA Tournament for the first time since 2022, scoring the 14th seed in the Midwest Region. The Raiders went 23–11 this season, including a 15–5 run in the Horizon League that culminated in Tuesday’s 66–63 comeback, conference championship win over Detroit Mercy. It’s the first time in program history that they captured both the regular-season and tournament titles in the same season. Clint Sargent’s conference-best offense is also one of the youngest; six players are averaging over eight points per game, and six of their top seven scorers are underclassmen. Friday’s showdown with the Cavaliers will be the Raiders’ first game against a nationally ranked opponent all season.

Virginia’s tournament outlook feels like the kind of March story the sport always claims to want: a blueblood with scar tissue, a first-year coach who has already changed the temperature in the room, and a team that arrives looking more dangerous in mid-March than it did in mid-January. The Cavaliers are 29-5, landed a No. 3 seed in the Midwest, and open against Wright State in Philadelphia after a week that included ACC tournament wins over NC State and Miami and a four-point title-game loss to Duke that looked much more like a warning than a failure. Ryan Odom’s group is no longer playing the old Virginia register either. This team has real scoring pop—around 81 points per game and 10.2 made threes—while still carrying the defensive nastiness that makes the uniform matter in March. Malik Thomas and Sam Lewis have become the perimeter pressure points, Thijs De Ridder made first-team All-ACC, and Ugonna Onyenso has turned into a full-on postseason menace, setting an ACC tournament record with 21 blocks over three games and ranking among the nation’s most disruptive rim protectors by block rate. The Cavaliers’ tournament hopes are real because the bracket gives them a clean runway into the second round before the violence gets heavier. Beat Wright State and Virginia likely gets Tennessee or a volatile First Four survivor. Get through that, and suddenly this stops being a comeback season and starts reading like a proper resurrection.

Santa Clara comes into this tournament with the exact energy of a band that spent years playing cult rooms and has suddenly been handed the festival sunset slot. The Broncos are 26-8, back in the NCAA tournament for the first time since 1996, and their résumé has the right kind of late-season glow: they won 13 of their last 16, beat Saint Mary’s in the WCC semifinal, and played their way into an at-large bid after a season that put Herb Sendek’s group squarely back on the national map. Statistically, they look sturdy enough to be dangerous—82.9 points per game, 35.7 rebounds, 16.8 assists, a plus-10.4 scoring margin, 46.8% shooting from the field, 10.1 made threes per game, and a 35.0% offensive rebounding rate that gives them lively second-chance bite instead of empty stylistic flair. In league play, they were even sharper from deep, leading the WCC at 10.4 made threes per game on 36.7% shooting, and they got 30 bench points per game, which ranked second in the conference and 27th nationally. Christian Hammond is still the headliner at 15.8 points per game, Elijah Mahi adds 13.9, and Allen Graves does a little bit of everything at 11.6 points, 6.5 rebounds, and 2.0 steals while shooting 41.6% from three. Their first matchup is Kentucky, which makes the vibe obvious immediately: this is one of the tournament’s better upset auditions. The Broncos are a confident, veteran-feeling offensive team with enough shotmaking and enough recent proof to make a brand-name favorite sweat. Their tournament hopes, then, are refreshingly clear. Santa Clara is here to see whether a 30-year drought can be punctuated with the kind of Thursday-or-Friday win that instantly rewrites how a season is remembered. Kentucky is vulnerable enough to make that plausible. The question is whether Santa Clara can keep the game in its own tempo long enough to turn plausibility into one of March’s annual little legends.

The Kentucky Wildcats’ tournament outlook feels like one of those prestige games that got greenlit on brand equity and then spent all winter trying to justify the budget. The Wildcats are 21-13, only seventh in the SEC standings, and their statistical profile is more solid than imperial: 80.8 points per game, 16 assists, 73.8 allowed. Otega Oweh is still the face of the rotation at 18.2 points a night, with Denzel Aberdeen handing out 3.6 assists and Malachi Moreno giving them 6.4 rebounds and 1.6 blocks per game, which is to say the parts are real even if the final cut has run uneven. Their first matchup is a dangerous one—No. 10 Santa Clara, a team that has spent the past week auditioning as the kind of WCC bracket spoiler America falls in love with by Thursday afternoon. Kentucky did at least grab a useful SEC tournament win over Missouri before Florida punked it again on the glass, and that’s the broader issue here: the Wildcats can absolutely win this first game, but their tournament hopes are less about a grand regional charge than about surviving the first stress test and proving they can control a game physically for 40 minutes. If they do, Iowa State likely waits next. If they don’t, this becomes another Kentucky March remembered as mood more than accomplishment.

The Tigers are dancing for the first time in 32 years, locking up the 15th seed in the Midwest Region and a date with No. 2 seed Iowa State in St. Louis. Under first-year head coach Nolan Smith, they went 23-9 and 15-5 in the Ohio Valley Conference—capping their run with a 26-point rout of Morehead State in the March 7 finale. Tennessee State plays at an enthusiastic tempo and leads the OVC in scoring; Aaron Nkrumah paces the conference with 17.6 points per game, while Travis Harper II adds 17.3 points with a conference-high 2.5 triples per contest. The Tigers played just one game against a ranked opponent this season, taking an 89-60 thumping from No. 20 Tennessee in November.

It was another terrific campaign in Ames; Iowa State ranks sixth on KenPom with a +32.36 net rating. With that being said, the past few weeks have been a bit shaky. The Cyclones have gone 4-4 during their last eight contests. That includes a brutal 82-80 defeat to Arizona in the Big 12 Tournament. Still, this is a team nobody wants to play even in the midst of a slump. T.J. Otzelberger’s guys have posted the nation’s fifth-best adjusted defensive efficiency (91.5). The offense is underrated too, knocking down threes at college basketball’s 11th-best rate (38.7%). To boot, the trio of Milan Momcilovic (17.1 PPG), Joshua Jefferson (16.9 PPG) and Tamin Lipsey (13.3 PPG) can beat opponents in a number of different ways. ISU has the necessary personnel for a trip to Indianapolis.

The LIU Sharks are taking the viral “Fins Up” celebration to San Diego, punching their first ticket to March Madness since 2018. Former Knicks guard Rod Strickland’s squad claimed the 16th seed in the West Region for a first-round matchup with the top-seeded Arizona Wildcats. LIU went 24-10 this season with a 15-3 mark in conference play, leading the NEC in scoring behind a formidable backcourt trio: All-NEC first team members Malachi Davis and Jamal Fuller, along with NEC Defensive Player of the Year and tournament MVP Greg Gordon. The Sharks also rank 10th nationally in blocks per game, bolstered by standout big man Shadrak Lasu.

Tommy Lloyd’s squad holds a 32-2 record this season, with its two losses coming against Kansas and Texas Tech. Arizona defeated Houston in the Big 12 Tournament Championship, showing impressive toughness in doing so. The Wildcats rank 14th in the country in scoring at 86.1 points per game, 54th in opponents’ points allowed, and in the top 17 in offensive and defensive ratings. Arizona primarily operates inside the three-point arc, ranking 358th in 3PA per game and second in 2PA, but has the big bodies to bang and ranks fourth in the country in rebounds per game. Brayden Burries (15.9 PPG and 4.7 RPG) leads the team in scoring, while Koa Peat (13.6 PPG and 5.3 RPG) and Tobe Awaka (9.4 PPG and 9.5 RPG) set the tone on the interior. Arizona is tough, battle-tested, and has made it to the regional semifinals of the NCAA Tournament in three of the last four years. It will surely be looking to match this and make an even deeper run this year.

The Mountain West champs put forth a fantastic campaign at 28-6 overall and 15-5 in conference play to earn their fourth consecutive March Madness bid. Utah State ranks 30th overall per KenPom and has been excellent on offense with 81.7 PPG and the 28th-best ORTG thanks to one of the country’s most efficient units. The Aggies shoot 49.5% from the field – 15th in the nation – and their ball movement looks good on the stat sheet with 17.2 assists per contest and a 1.625 AST/TO ratio which both fall in the top 25. The star duo of MJ Collins Jr. (17.6 PPG) and Mason Falslev (16.1 PPG) power this team on a nightly basis. Defensively, Utah State is slightly weaker with 70.8 PPG allowed and the 45th-ranked DRTG, though those aren’t bad marks. Rebounding is the team’s biggest weakness, so larger lineups could cause issues against this group. Still, these Aggies are a name to keep an eye on.

After leading Maryland to the regional semifinals last year, Kevin Willard jumped to the Big East and snapped Villanova’s three-year NCAA Tournament drought. Willard did an excellent job attacking the transfer portal, and the Wildcats finished with a 24-8 record on the year. Tyler Perkins (13.7 points and 5.4 rebounds) is the team’s leading scorer, while Grand Canyon transfer Duke Brennan (12.4 points and 10.3 rebounds) is essential for setting the tone on the interior, and freshman Acaden Lewis (12.3 points and 5.3 assists) pulls the strings of the offense. Unfortunately, Villanova received a tough blow with three games remaining in the regular season, with Matt Hodge (9.2 points and 3.6 rebounds) suffering a torn ACL. Hodge does not shine in the stat sheet, but was responsible for doing plenty of the dirty work and was recognized as a leader on the team. Villanova can get hot from deep and attempt the 45th-most three-pointers in the country but grades out in the middle of the pack in most of their overall metrics. The Wildcats finished the season with a sour taste in their mouths as they were eliminated by Georgetown in the opening round of the Big East tournament in what was their worst loss of the season. They will use the time off to try to rekindle their early-season spark and get back to playing their best basketball without Hodge as a part of that unit.

High Point arrives with the exact statistical profile that makes a 12-seed feel less like folklore and more like design. The Panthers are 30-4, went 15-1 in the Big South, and won the league tournament by flattening Winthrop 91-76. They also score 90.0 points per game—sixth nationally—while handing out 16.3 assists and allowing only 70.3. That is a very real offense. The advanced-stat version makes the same point with even less romance: High Point shot 49.1% from the field and 35.6% from three, posted roughly a 56.6% effective field goal rate, got to the line at about a 43.3% free-throw rate, and paired that scoring pop with only 9.4 turnovers per game, a 1.7 assist-turnover ratio, and a staggering plus-7.1 turnover margin. They also forced 16.4 turnovers per game, generated 21.2 points off turnovers, and held opponents to 42.6% shooting and 31.7% from deep, which is why this team reads more like an engineered upset profile than a one-bid curiosity. Terry Anderson leads them with 16.0 points per game, Rob Martin is both a scorer and organizer, and Owen Aquino brings rim protection with 1.7 blocks per game. Even the conference-title game read like a declaration: Martin went for 24, Cam’Ron Fletcher ripped down 19 rebounds, and High Point turned the whole thing into a celebration by mid-second half. Their first matchup is Wisconsin, which means the upset narrative is already writing itself in the margins of thousands of brackets. The tournament hopes here are obvious but not delusional. High Point is the kind of team that can absolutely win one because it can score with structure rather than miracle shotmaking. The catch is what comes next. This region is terrifically unmerciful. Arkansas and then maybe Arizona wait down the hallway, and those are very different forms of basketball violence. So the Panthers’ cleanest dream is probably the classic one: win the opener, steal the national mood for 24 hours, and make a power-conference fan base explain why 90 points per game wasn’t supposed to mean anything just because it happened in the Big South.

Wisconsin showed its ceiling in the Big Ten Tournament. The Badgers are 24-10, went 14-6 in the Big Ten, grabbed a No. 5 seed in the West, and head to Portland for a first-round date with High Point after a closing stretch that included wins over Purdue, Washington and Illinois before a 68-65 semifinal loss to Michigan. The profile is not glamorous so much as ruthlessly coherent: 83 points per game, 45% shooting, 36.1% from three, 78.6% at the line, 16 assists against just 8.9 turnovers, and 11.8 made threes per night. Using Wisconsin’s official team totals, that offense works out to about a 54.5% effective field goal rate, which is exactly the kind of modern math that keeps a team from ever really looking rushed. The whole thing is built around a backcourt that can turn a tense game into a shooting gallery before anybody notices the room temperature changing. Nick Boyd is a livewire at 20.6 points, 3.8 rebounds, and 36 steals while shooting 47.9% from the field and 82.4% from the line, and he’s peaking at the right time. John Blackwell adds 19 points and 4.9 rebounds with 93 made threes at 38.4%; Nolan Winter brings the frontcourt ballast at 13.3 points and 8.6 rebounds on 56.9% shooting. Wisconsin’s tournament hope is simple and very Wisconsin: let the spacing, decision-making, and shotmaking do the slow work of suffocation. When the Badgers keep the ball moving and the threes falling, they look like one of those teams that survive while flashier neighbors self-destruct.

Hawai'i feels like one of the more intriguing lower seeds because the profile is less gimmick than grit. The Rainbow Warriors are 24-8, finished 14-6 in the Big West, and finally broke through for their first NCAA berth since 2016 by beating UC Irvine 71-64 in the title game after knocking off Cal State Fullerton in the semifinals. The emotional shape of that run matters. So does the way they play. Hawai'i scores 79.6 points per game, rebounds extremely well at 39.3 per night, and allows only 69.7. The Rainbow Warriors have played at about 74.5 possessions per game, posted a 1.057 offensive efficiency and a 0.944 defensive efficiency, held opponents to a 46.4% effective field goal rate, 46.6% shooting on twos, and 30.7% from three, while cleaning up 77.2% of available defensive rebounds. Offensively, they have generated about a 52.0% effective field goal rate, hit 55.6% on twos, taken roughly 40% of their shots from deep, and gotten to the line at a healthy clip, which is why the identity reads sturdier than the seed line might suggest. Isaac Johnson leads the team with 14.1 points per game, Hunter Erickson supplies 3.8 assists, and Dre Bullock contributes both on the glass and defensively. Their first matchup is Arkansas, which is the sort of draw that tells a lower seed to be either excellent immediately or gone by dinner. The tournament hopes here are still very palpable, though, because Hawai'i is both fun and annoying in ways that generate wins. It already rebounds, already defends, already looks comfortable playing games that get a little heavier and less decorative. That is often enough to drag a favorite into a very unwelcome kind of first-round afternoon. The issue is ceiling. Arkansas has more top-end talent and more ways to survive a bad half. So Hawai'i’s best path is the oldest one in the book: turn this into a half-court argument, own the glass, and make the team with more stars prove it can actually play a forty-minute tournament game instead of just posing as the better roster.

The Razorbacks won the SEC Tournament for the second time in program history thanks to a dynamic backcourt of Darius Acuff Jr. and Meleek Thomas. The two freshmen are the conductors of the sixth ranked offense on KenPom, so don’t try to outscore them. Arkansas averages the fourth most points per game in Division I, and has failed to hit 80 points in just seven games this season. Defense is a different story, as the Razorbacks rank 48th on KenPom’s defensive rating. Whether the defense improves in the NCAA Tournament will be something to watch. That’ll be key to Arkansas winning its second-ever NCAA championship and first since 1994.

BYU arrives with the vibe of a blockbuster that absolutely has a star, absolutely has spectacle, and still leaves critics arguing about whether the sky's truly the limit. The Cougars are 23-11, went 9-9 in the Big 12, earned a No. 6 seed in the West, and will open in Portland against the winner of Texas-NC State with Gonzaga lurking as the sort of second-round reunion the committee loves because it feels prewritten. The team profile is loud enough to justify the seed and weird enough to make the ceiling hard to read cleanly: 83.9 points per game, 47.7% shooting, 34.9% from three, 74.6% at the line, 38.3 rebounds, 13.5 assists, 7.2 steals, 4.4 blocks, and only 10.9 turnovers. They have also gone 8-2 on neutral floors, which matters because this team tends to look most convincing when the game turns into a talent-forward event rather than a long ideological argument. And then there is NBA-lottery-bound AJ Dybantsa, who has spent the season functioning like a program's entire hopes. He is at 25.3 points, 6.7 rebounds, and 3.8 assists on 51.3% shooting, while Robert Wright III gives BYU a second serious creator at 18.2 points, 4.7 assists, and 42.2% from three. Keba Keita rounds the thing out with 7.3 rebounds, 1.7 blocks, and 67.7% shooting, which is how the Cougars keep the whole operation from floating off into pure perimeter theater. The recent receipt is absurd in exactly the right way: Dybantsa just dropped a Big 12 tournament-record 93 points over three games, including 40 against Kansas State and 26 against Houston in the quarterfinal loss. That is why BYU’s tournament hope never has to be explained twice. The volatility is legit, but so is the star power. When Dybantsa catches fire and Wright keeps the offense from becoming a one-man trailer, BYU stops looking like a six seed and starts looking like the kind of team that can hijack a weekend before the bracket has time to object.

Ah, the Owls. Kennesaw State comes in at 163rd per KenPom after going 21-13 overall and 10-10 in Conference USA play. They entered the conference tournament as a No. 6 seed but shockingly went on to win the whole thing, securing their bid to the Big Dance. While the Owls’ 80.5 PPG are solid and they get to the charity stripe more than any team in the country, the 78.4 PPG allowed on the opposite end are far from inspiring. Sure, they’re also pretty good on the boards at 27th in rebounding while also sitting ninth in blocks, but sloppy play is something of an issue at 250th in turnovers and near dead last at the Division I level in foul rate.Simeon Cottle’s 20.2 PPG make him one of the nation’s higher-upside scorers, but there are flaws that will likely prove fatal unless this hot streak continues.

Mark Few’s squad cruised to a 30-3 record this season, with the three losses coming against Michigan, Portland and Saint Mary’s. The Bulldogs finished the season by winning the West Coast Conference and ending ranked 12th in the AP Poll. Gonzaga ranks 17th in the country in scoring, 18th in opponents’ points allowed, 15th in offensive rating and is posting the best defensive rating in the country. Graham Ike (19.7 PPG and 8.2 RPG) headlines the production, while Grand Canyon transfer Tyon Grant-Foster (11.2 PPG and 5.0 RPG) has scaled up his production as the season has progressed. Strength of schedule concerns and memories of past Gonzaga upsets will stick in some minds, but the Bulldogs are tied with Duke for the best average margin of victory in college basketball (+19.1). You can only beat who is in front of you, and Gonzaga has done this at as high a level as any team this year and will carry this into the NCAA Tournament.

The Tigers finished the season with a 20-12 record, collecting some impressive wins along the way in SEC play. Missouri was able to upset Florida, Kentucky, Vanderbilt, Tennessee and Texas A&M, but also lost to teams like Notre Dame, and SEC bottomfeeders in LSU and Ole Miss. From a metrics standpoint, Missouri is one of the lowest ranked teams to make the field as an at-large bid, sitting at 52nd on KenPom. Ranking 78th in defensive efficiency on KenPom tells us that the Tigers tend to struggle on that end of the floor. But offensively, they are led by senior Mark Mitchell, who’s able to do it all. Mitchell averages over 18 points, 5.3 rebounds and 3.6 assists while knocking down over 50% of his shots. Having made deep NCAA Tournament runs during his time at Duke, Mitchell has the experience that could help lead Missouri in March.

The U is officially back on the national stage in football, but that may ring true on the hardwood as well. Miami just went 25-8 overall and 13-5 in the ACC but received what feels like very little national acclaim in the process. The Hurricanes are 31st in the KenPom rankings and have a very productive offense that averages 81.9 PPG while shooting 50.1% overall, the 10th-best FG% in the country. They’re also solid on the glass and particularly capable on the offensive boards with the 30th-ranked OREB% as well. There’s plenty of production from Malik Reneau (18.8 PPG, 6.6 REB) and Tre Donaldson (16.5 PPG), plus another pair of double-digit scorers. The defense is a little bit shakier at 38th in DRTG, but there’s a lot to like about this Miami group as a potential dark horse to make a run.

Queens comes into this tournament with the exact kind of first-act chaos March loves .The Royals are 21-13, won the ASUN tournament as the No. 3 seed, and reached the NCAA field in their very first year of full Division I eligibility, which is already the sort of résumé detail that makes a lower seed feel more mythic than modest. Their title game was a little piece of instant-school-history cinema too: Queens outlasted top-seeded Central Arkansas 98-93 in overtime behind 34 points and 10 made threes from Chris Ashby, sealing the program’s first ASUN tournament crown and first NCAA berth in the D-I era. The first matchup is brutal in the purest bracket sense—No. 15 Queens against No. 2 Purdue in St. Louis—which means the tournament hope is not some dreamy long runway. It is one loud night, one hot shooting spell, one game where the favorite has to keep looking down and realizing the underdog did not come to pose. The reason Queens is at least interesting is that the offense has legit voltage. The Royals score 84.9 points per game, shoot 48.2% from the field, hit 36.0% from three, and make 10.2 threes a night while averaging 15.9 assists. They are total-unit act, too: Nasir Mann leads at 13.4 points and 5.8 rebounds per game, Jordan Watford adds 11.9 points and 3.8 assists, Avantae Parker scores 11.3 a night while shooting 68.5% from the field, and Ashby’s title-game explosion reminded everyone how quickly this team can turn a game into a scoreboard emergency. The warning label is obvious too. Queens gives up 82.9 points per game, allows opponents to shoot 46.6% overall and 35.4% from deep, and lives in the kind of high-variance environment that can look charming until it runs into Purdue’s size and structure. But that is also the whole romance of a team like this. All Queens needs is to be explosive enough to make the first round feel weird.

The Purdue Boilermakers have momentum on their side, defeating Michigan to win the Big Ten Tournament and entering on a four-game win streak. Matt Painter’s squad is 27-8 and finished ranked 18th in the AP Poll. This is an experienced squad with 69.6% of the minutes played from last year’s roster and 79.6% of last year’s scoring production back on this year’s team. That’s become increasingly rare in this college basketball era. Braden Smith (14 PPG and 9.0 APG), Fletcher Loyer (13.8 PPG) and Trey Kaufman-Renn (13.4 PPG and 8.7 RPG) headline the production and are each in their fourth season with the program. Oscar Cluff (10.3 PPG and 7.4 RPG) also plays a vital role in setting the tone on the interior and has been a necessary addition this year. Purdue ranks 55th in the country in scoring, second in offensive rating, 16th in field goal percentage, and 17th in three-point percentage. The Boilermakers lost in the NCAA Championship game in 2023-24 with much of the same team and will be eager to get back to it.
